nodes.name: (X,r,k)-factor
nodes.statement:
Let $r$ and $k$ be positive integers and \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph. Let 
\(X\subset V\) and \(F \subset E\).
	We say that \(F\) is an \emph{\((X,r,k)\)-factor} of 
\(G\) if, for every \(v\in X\), we have \(d_F(v) = (r/k)d_G(v)\).
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: (X,l,k)-fractional factorization
nodes.statement_short: A partition of $E$ into $\ell$ $(X,1,k)$-factors and $(k-\ell)/2$ Eulerian $(X,2,k)$-factors.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Fractional factorization forces divisible degrees
nodes.statement:
Note that, if \(G\) contains an \((X,1,k)\)-factor, then \(d_G(v)\) is 
divisible by $k$ for every \(v\in X\). Therefore, 
this fact implies that, if \(G\) admits an \((X,\ell,k)\)-fractional 
factorization, 
then \(d(v)\) is divisible by \(k\) for every \(v\in X\).
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations
conclusions: \(d(v)\) is divisible by \(k\) for every \(v\in X\)

nodes.name: Existence of (A,1,2k+1)-fractional factorizations
nodes.statement:
Let \(k\) be a positive integer.
If $G=(A,B;E)$ is a $2k$-edge-connected bipartite graph such that $d_G(v)$ is 
divisible by $2k+1$ for every 
$v\in A$, then $G$ admits an \((A,1,2k+1)\)-fractional factorization.
assumptions:
$d_G(v)$ is 
divisible by $2k+1$ for every 
$v\in A$
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations
nodes.label: lemma:1-special-decomposition

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.3
nodes.statement:
Let \(G=(A,B;E)\) be as in the hypothesis.
First, we want to apply Lemma~\ref{lemma:splitting-of-vertices} to obtain a 
\(2k\)-edge-connected graph $G'$ 
with maximum degree \(4k-1\).
To do this, for every vertex $v \in B$, we take integers $s_v \geq 1$ and $0 \leq r_v < 2k$ 
such that $d_G(v) = 2ks_v + r_v$.
We put $d^v_1 = 2k+r_v$ and \(d^v_2 = \cdots = d^v_{s_v} = 2k\).
Furthermore, for every 
vertex $v\in A$, we put $s_v=d_G(v)/(2k+1)$ and $d^v_i=2k+1$ for $1\leq i\leq s_v$.
By Lemma~\ref{lemma:splitting-of-vertices} 
(applied with parameters $2k$ and the integers $s_v$, $d^v_i$ ($1\leq i\leq 
s_v$) for every $v\in V(G)$), there exists a 
$2k$-edge-connected bipartite graph $G'$ obtained from \(G\) by splitting each 
vertex \(v\) of \(A\) into \(s_v\) 
vertices of degree \(2k+1\), and each vertex \(v\) of \(B\) into a 
vertex of
degree $2k+r_v < 4k$ and $s_v-1$ vertices of degree $2k$.
Let \(A'\) and \(B'\) be the set of vertices of \(G'\) obtained from 
the vertices of \(A\) and \(B\),
respectively. 
For ease of notation, if \(v \in (A' \cup B') \setminus (A \cup B)\) we also 
denote by \(v\) the vertex in \(A \cup B\) that gave rise to $v$.

The next step is to obtain a $(2k+1)$-regular multigraph $G^*$ from $G'$ by 
using lifting operations. For this, we 
will add some edges to $A'$ and remove the even-degree vertices of $B'$ by successive
applications of Mader's Lifting Theorem as 
follows.
Let \(G'_0,G'_1,\ldots,G'_\lambda\) be a maximal sequence of graphs such that \(G'_0 = G'\)
and (for \(i\geq 0\)) \(G'_{i+1}\) is the graph obtained from \(G'_i\) 
by the application of an admissible lifting 
at an arbitrary vertex \(v\) with $d_{G'}(v)\notin \{1,2,2k+1\}$.



Recall that, given any two distinct vertices of \(G'\), say \(x\) and \(y\), we denote by \(p_{G'}(x,y)\)
the maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint paths joining \(x\) and \(y\) in \({G'}\).
We claim that \(p_{G'_i}(x,y) \geq 2k\) for any \(x,y\) in \(A'\) and every \(i\geq 0\).
Clearly, \(p_{G'_0}(x,y) \geq 2k\) holds for any \(x,y\) in \(A'\), since \(G'\) is \(2k\)-edge-connected.
Fix \(i\geq 0\) and suppose \(p_{G'_i}(x,y) \geq 2k\) holds for any \(x,y\) in \(A'\).
Let \(x,y\) be two vertices in \(A'\).
Since \(G'_{i+1}\) is a graph obtained from \(G'_i\) by the application 
of an admissible lifting at a vertex \(v\) in \(B'\), 
we have \(p_{G'_{i+1}}(x,y) \geq p_{G'_i}(x,y) \geq 2k\).

We claim that, if \(v\in B'\)
then \(d_{G'_\lambda}(v) \in \{2,2k+1\}\).
Suppose, for a contradiction, that there is a vertex \(v\) in \(B'\) 
such that \(d_{G'_\lambda}(v) \notin \{2,2k+1\}\).
Note that \(d_{G'_i}(u) \geq d_{G'_{i+1}}(u)\geq 2\)
for every \(u\in V(G')\) and every \(0\leq i\leq \lambda\).
Since \(d_{G'}(u) \leq 4k-1\) for every \(u\in V(G')\),
we have \(2\leq d_{G'_i}(u)\leq 4k-1\) for every \(0\leq i\leq \lambda\).
Therefore, \(2\leq d_{G'_\lambda}(v)\leq 4k-1\).
Since \(d_{G'_\lambda}(v) \leq 4k-1\),
and for any two neighbors $x$ and $y$ of \(v\) we have \(p_{G'_\lambda}(x,y)\geq 2k\),
Lemma~\ref{lemma:non-cut-vertex} implies that \(v\) is not a cut-vertex of \(G'_\lambda\).
Then, by Mader's Lifting Theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:Mader}) applied to \(G'_\lambda\),
there is an admissible lifting at \(v\).
Therefore, \(G'_0,G'_1,\ldots,G'_\lambda\) is not maximal, a contradiction.



In \(G'_\lambda\) the set $B'$ may have some vertices of degree $2$. 
For every such vertex $v$, if $u$ and $w$ are the neighbours of $v$, we apply a \(uw\)-lifting at $v$, 
and remove the vertex $v$, i.e, we perform a supression of \(v\).
Let \(G^*\) be the graph obtained by applying this process to all vertices of degree $2$ in $B'$.
Note that the number of pairwise edge-disjoint paths joining two distinct vertices of \(A'\)
remains the same, i.e, \(p_{G^*}(x,y) \geq p_{G_\lambda}(x,y)\geq 2k\) for every \(x,y\) in \(A'\).
Clearly, the 
set of vertices of $G^*$ that belong to $B'$ is an independent set;  
we denote it by $B^*$  (eventually, \(B^* = \emptyset\)). 
Furthermore, every vertex in \(B^*\) has degree \(2k+1\).


\begin{claim}
\(G^*\) is \(2k\)-edge connected.
\end{claim}
\begin{proof}
Let \(Y \subset V(G^*)\).
Suppose there is at least one vertex \(x\) of \(A'\) in \(Y\)
and at least one vertex \(y\) of \(A'\) in \(V(G^*)-Y\).
Since there are at least \(2k\) edge-disjoint paths joining \(x\) to \(y\),
there are at least \(2k\) edges with vertices in both \(Y\) and 
\(V(G^*)-Y\).
Now, suppose that \(A'\subset Y\) (otherwise \(A'\subset V(G^*)-Y\) and
we take \(V(G^*)-Y\) instead of \(Y\)), and then \(V(G^*)-Y \subset B^*\).
Since \(B^*\) is an independent set, all edges with a vertex in \(V(G^*)-Y\) 
must have the other vertex in \(A'\).
Since every vertex in \(B^*\) has degree \(2k+1\), 
there are at least \(2k+1\) edges with vertices in both \(Y\) and \(V(G^*)-Y\). 
\end{proof}

We conclude that $G^*$ is a 
$2k$-edge-connected $(2k+1)$-regular multigraph with vertex-set $A'\cup B^*$, 
where $B^*$ is an independent set.


Since every vertex of \(G^*\) has odd degree, $|V(G^*)|$ is even.
Thus, \(G^*\) is a \(2k\)-edge-connected 
\((2k+1)\)-regular multigraph of even order. 
By Theorem~\ref{thm:Kano}, \(G^*\) contains a perfect matching \(M^*\).
Since the multigraph \(J^* = G^* - M^*\)  
is \(2k\)-regular, Theorem~\ref{thm:Petersen} implies that \(J^*\) admits a decomposition 
into \(2\)-factors, say \(F^*_1,\ldots,F^*_k\).
Therefore, \(M^*,F^*_1,\ldots,F^*_k\) is a partition of \(E(G^*)\).


Now, let us get back to the bipartite graph $G$. 
Let \(xy\) be an edge of \(G^*\).
If $x\in A'$ and $y\in B^*$, 
then \(xy\) corresponds to an edge of \(G\). On the other hand, if \(x,y\in A'\),
then there is a vertex \(v_{xy}\) of \(B'\) and two edges 
\(xv_{xy}\) and \(v_{xy}y\) in $E(G')$. Furthermore,
\(xy\) was obtained by an \(xy\)-lifting 
at \(v_{xy}\) (either by an application of Mader's Lifting 
Theorem or by the supression of vertices of degree $2$).
Then, each edge of \(G^*\) represents an edge of \(G\) or a \(2\)-path
in \(G\) such that the internal vertices of these \(2\)-paths are 
always 
in \(B\).
For every edge $xy\in E(G^*)$, define \(f(xy) = \{xy\}\) if $x\in A'$ and $y\in B^*$,
and \(f(xy) = \{xv_{xy},v_{xy}y\}\) if \(x,y\in A'\). Note that $f(xy)\subset E(G)$ for every edge $xy\in E(G^*)$.
For a set \(S\subset E(G^*)\), put \(f(S) = \cup_{e\in S} f(e)\).
The partition of \(E(G^*)\) into \(M^*,F^*_1,\ldots,F^*_k\) induces 
a partition of \(E(G)\) into \(M = f(M^*)\) and \(F_i = f(F^*_i)\) for $1\leq i\leq k$.


We will prove that \(\{M,F_1,\ldots,F_k\}\) is an \((A,1,2k+1)\)-fractional 
factorization. Fix $i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$. We will show that \(M\) is an \((A,1,2k+1)\)-factor of $G$ 
and \(F_i\) is an Eulerian \((A,2,2k+1)\)-factor of $G$.
Let \(v\) be a vertex of \(A\) in \(G\) and put \(d'(v) = d(v)/(2k+1)\). Then, we know that 
\(v\) is represented by \(d'(v)\) vertices in \(G^*\).
Since \(M^*\) is a perfect matching in \(G^*\), there are \(d'(v)\) edges
of \(M\) entering \(v\) and, since \(F^*_i\) is a \(2\)-factor in \(G^*\),
there are \(2d'(v)\) edges of \(F_i\) incident to \(v\).
Finally, since \(F^*_i\) is Eulerian, the set
\(F_i\) is Eulerian, concluding the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Split vertices (Lemma 2.1), lift away $B$-side vertices with Mader's theorem to get a $2k$-edge-connected $(2k+1)$-regular multigraph, take a perfect matching and Petersen 2-factors, and pull back to $G$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Plan
nodes.statement:
Let \(G=(A,B;E)\) be as in the hypothesis.
First, we want to apply Lemma~\ref{lemma:splitting-of-vertices} to obtain a 
\(2k\)-edge-connected graph $G'$ 
with maximum degree \(4k-1\).
nodes.statement_short: First obtain a $2k$-edge-connected detachment of maximum degree $4k-1$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Choose subdegree sequences
nodes.statement:
To do this, for every vertex $v \in B$, we take integers $s_v \geq 1$ and $0 \leq r_v < 2k$ 
such that $d_G(v) = 2ks_v + r_v$.
We put $d^v_1 = 2k+r_v$ and \(d^v_2 = \cdots = d^v_{s_v} = 2k\).
Furthermore, for every 
vertex $v\in A$, we put $s_v=d_G(v)/(2k+1)$ and $d^v_i=2k+1$ for $1\leq i\leq s_v$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose subdegree sequences: parts $2k$ (plus remainder) on $B$, parts $2k+1$ on $A$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Apply splitting lemma
nodes.statement:
By Lemma~\ref{lemma:splitting-of-vertices} 
(applied with parameters $2k$ and the integers $s_v$, $d^v_i$ ($1\leq i\leq 
s_v$) for every $v\in V(G)$), there exists a 
$2k$-edge-connected bipartite graph $G'$ obtained from \(G\) by splitting each 
vertex \(v\) of \(A\) into \(s_v\) 
vertices of degree \(2k+1\), and each vertex \(v\) of \(B\) into a 
vertex of
degree $2k+r_v < 4k$ and $s_v-1$ vertices of degree $2k$.
Let \(A'\) and \(B'\) be the set of vertices of \(G'\) obtained from 
the vertices of \(A\) and \(B\),
respectively. 
For ease of notation, if \(v \in (A' \cup B') \setminus (A \cup B)\) we also 
denote by \(v\) the vertex in \(A \cup B\) that gave rise to $v$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2.1 gives a $2k$-edge-connected bipartite detachment $G'$ with vertex sets $A'$, $B'$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Maximal lifting sequence
nodes.statement:
The next step is to obtain a $(2k+1)$-regular multigraph $G^*$ from $G'$ by 
using lifting operations. For this, we 
will add some edges to $A'$ and remove the even-degree vertices of $B'$ by successive
applications of Mader's Lifting Theorem as 
follows.
Let \(G'_0,G'_1,\ldots,G'_\lambda\) be a maximal sequence of graphs such that \(G'_0 = G'\)
and (for \(i\geq 0\)) \(G'_{i+1}\) is the graph obtained from \(G'_i\) 
by the application of an admissible lifting 
at an arbitrary vertex \(v\) with $d_{G'}(v)\notin \{1,2,2k+1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a maximal sequence of admissible liftings at vertices of degree not in $\{1,2,2k+1\}$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Recall p_G
nodes.statement:
Recall that, given any two distinct vertices of \(G'\), say \(x\) and \(y\), we denote by \(p_{G'}(x,y)\)
the maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint paths joining \(x\) and \(y\) in \({G'}\).
nodes.statement_short: Recall $p_{G'}(x,y)$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Connectivity between A' vertices preserved
nodes.statement:
We claim that \(p_{G'_i}(x,y) \geq 2k\) for any \(x,y\) in \(A'\) and every \(i\geq 0\).
Clearly, \(p_{G'_0}(x,y) \geq 2k\) holds for any \(x,y\) in \(A'\), since \(G'\) is \(2k\)-edge-connected.
Fix \(i\geq 0\) and suppose \(p_{G'_i}(x,y) \geq 2k\) holds for any \(x,y\) in \(A'\).
Let \(x,y\) be two vertices in \(A'\).
Since \(G'_{i+1}\) is a graph obtained from \(G'_i\) by the application 
of an admissible lifting at a vertex \(v\) in \(B'\), 
we have \(p_{G'_{i+1}}(x,y) \geq p_{G'_i}(x,y) \geq 2k\).
nodes.statement_short: By induction on $i$, $p_{G'_i}(x,y)\ge 2k$ for $x,y\in A'$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Base and hypothesis
nodes.statement:
Clearly, \(p_{G'_0}(x,y) \geq 2k\) holds for any \(x,y\) in \(A'\), since \(G'\) is \(2k\)-edge-connected.
Fix \(i\geq 0\) and suppose \(p_{G'_i}(x,y) \geq 2k\) holds for any \(x,y\) in \(A'\).
nodes.statement_short: Base case $i=0$ from $2k$-edge-connectivity; assume for $i$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Admissible lifting step
nodes.statement:
Let \(x,y\) be two vertices in \(A'\).
Since \(G'_{i+1}\) is a graph obtained from \(G'_i\) by the application 
of an admissible lifting at a vertex \(v\) in \(B'\), 
we have \(p_{G'_{i+1}}(x,y) \geq p_{G'_i}(x,y) \geq 2k\).
nodes.statement_short: An admissible lifting at a $B'$ vertex does not decrease $p$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Degrees in B' end in {2,2k+1}
nodes.statement:
We claim that, if \(v\in B'\)
then \(d_{G'_\lambda}(v) \in \{2,2k+1\}\).
Suppose, for a contradiction, that there is a vertex \(v\) in \(B'\) 
such that \(d_{G'_\lambda}(v) \notin \{2,2k+1\}\).
Note that \(d_{G'_i}(u) \geq d_{G'_{i+1}}(u)\geq 2\)
for every \(u\in V(G')\) and every \(0\leq i\leq \lambda\).
Since \(d_{G'}(u) \leq 4k-1\) for every \(u\in V(G')\),
we have \(2\leq d_{G'_i}(u)\leq 4k-1\) for every \(0\leq i\leq \lambda\).
Therefore, \(2\leq d_{G'_\lambda}(v)\leq 4k-1\).
Since \(d_{G'_\lambda}(v) \leq 4k-1\),
and for any two neighbors $x$ and $y$ of \(v\) we have \(p_{G'_\lambda}(x,y)\geq 2k\),
Lemma~\ref{lemma:non-cut-vertex} implies that \(v\) is not a cut-vertex of \(G'_\lambda\).
Then, by Mader's Lifting Theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:Mader}) applied to \(G'_\lambda\),
there is an admissible lifting at \(v\).
Therefore, \(G'_0,G'_1,\ldots,G'_\lambda\) is not maximal, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: At the end of the lifting sequence every $B'$ vertex has degree 2 or $2k+1$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Assume a bad vertex
nodes.statement:
Suppose, for a contradiction, that there is a vertex \(v\) in \(B'\) 
such that \(d_{G'_\lambda}(v) \notin \{2,2k+1\}\).
nodes.statement_short: Suppose some $v\in B'$ has another degree.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Degree bounds
nodes.statement:
Note that \(d_{G'_i}(u) \geq d_{G'_{i+1}}(u)\geq 2\)
for every \(u\in V(G')\) and every \(0\leq i\leq \lambda\).
Since \(d_{G'}(u) \leq 4k-1\) for every \(u\in V(G')\),
we have \(2\leq d_{G'_i}(u)\leq 4k-1\) for every \(0\leq i\leq \lambda\).
Therefore, \(2\leq d_{G'_\lambda}(v)\leq 4k-1\).
nodes.statement_short: Degrees stay in $[2,4k-1]$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: v is not a cut-vertex
nodes.statement:
Since \(d_{G'_\lambda}(v) \leq 4k-1\),
and for any two neighbors $x$ and $y$ of \(v\) we have \(p_{G'_\lambda}(x,y)\geq 2k\),
Lemma~\ref{lemma:non-cut-vertex} implies that \(v\) is not a cut-vertex of \(G'_\lambda\).
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2.3 shows $v$ is not a cut-vertex.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Further lifting exists
nodes.statement:
Then, by Mader's Lifting Theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:Mader}) applied to \(G'_\lambda\),
there is an admissible lifting at \(v\).
Therefore, \(G'_0,G'_1,\ldots,G'_\lambda\) is not maximal, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Mader's theorem gives another admissible lifting, contradicting maximality.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Suppress degree-2 vertices
nodes.statement:
In \(G'_\lambda\) the set $B'$ may have some vertices of degree $2$. 
For every such vertex $v$, if $u$ and $w$ are the neighbours of $v$, we apply a \(uw\)-lifting at $v$, 
and remove the vertex $v$, i.e, we perform a supression of \(v\).
Let \(G^*\) be the graph obtained by applying this process to all vertices of degree $2$ in $B'$.
nodes.statement_short: Suppress the degree-2 vertices of $B'$ to obtain $G^*$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Properties of G*
nodes.statement:
Note that the number of pairwise edge-disjoint paths joining two distinct vertices of \(A'\)
remains the same, i.e, \(p_{G^*}(x,y) \geq p_{G_\lambda}(x,y)\geq 2k\) for every \(x,y\) in \(A'\).
Clearly, the 
set of vertices of $G^*$ that belong to $B'$ is an independent set;  
we denote it by $B^*$  (eventually, \(B^* = \emptyset\)). 
Furthermore, every vertex in \(B^*\) has degree \(2k+1\).
nodes.statement_short: $p_{G^*}\ge 2k$ on $A'$; $B^*$ is independent with all degrees $2k+1$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Claim 4.4
nodes.statement:
\begin{claim}
\(G^*\) is \(2k\)-edge connected.
\end{claim}
\begin{proof}
Let \(Y \subset V(G^*)\).
Suppose there is at least one vertex \(x\) of \(A'\) in \(Y\)
and at least one vertex \(y\) of \(A'\) in \(V(G^*)-Y\).
Since there are at least \(2k\) edge-disjoint paths joining \(x\) to \(y\),
there are at least \(2k\) edges with vertices in both \(Y\) and 
\(V(G^*)-Y\).
Now, suppose that \(A'\subset Y\) (otherwise \(A'\subset V(G^*)-Y\) and
we take \(V(G^*)-Y\) instead of \(Y\)), and then \(V(G^*)-Y \subset B^*\).
Since \(B^*\) is an independent set, all edges with a vertex in \(V(G^*)-Y\) 
must have the other vertex in \(A'\).
Since every vertex in \(B^*\) has degree \(2k+1\), 
there are at least \(2k+1\) edges with vertices in both \(Y\) and \(V(G^*)-Y\). 
\end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Claim 4.4 ($G^*$ is $2k$-edge-connected) and its proof.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: G* regular of even order
nodes.statement:
We conclude that $G^*$ is a 
$2k$-edge-connected $(2k+1)$-regular multigraph with vertex-set $A'\cup B^*$, 
where $B^*$ is an independent set.


Since every vertex of \(G^*\) has odd degree, $|V(G^*)|$ is even.
Thus, \(G^*\) is a \(2k\)-edge-connected 
\((2k+1)\)-regular multigraph of even order.
nodes.statement_short: $G^*$ is a $2k$-edge-connected $(2k+1)$-regular multigraph of even order.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Matching and 2-factors
nodes.statement:
By Theorem~\ref{thm:Kano}, \(G^*\) contains a perfect matching \(M^*\).
Since the multigraph \(J^* = G^* - M^*\)  
is \(2k\)-regular, Theorem~\ref{thm:Petersen} implies that \(J^*\) admits a decomposition 
into \(2\)-factors, say \(F^*_1,\ldots,F^*_k\).
Therefore, \(M^*,F^*_1,\ldots,F^*_k\) is a partition of \(E(G^*)\).
nodes.statement_short: Von Baebler gives a perfect matching; Petersen splits the rest into 2-factors.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Edges of G* as paths in G
nodes.statement:
Now, let us get back to the bipartite graph $G$. 
Let \(xy\) be an edge of \(G^*\).
If $x\in A'$ and $y\in B^*$, 
then \(xy\) corresponds to an edge of \(G\). On the other hand, if \(x,y\in A'\),
then there is a vertex \(v_{xy}\) of \(B'\) and two edges 
\(xv_{xy}\) and \(v_{xy}y\) in $E(G')$. Furthermore,
\(xy\) was obtained by an \(xy\)-lifting 
at \(v_{xy}\) (either by an application of Mader's Lifting 
Theorem or by the supression of vertices of degree $2$).
Then, each edge of \(G^*\) represents an edge of \(G\) or a \(2\)-path
in \(G\) such that the internal vertices of these \(2\)-paths are 
always 
in \(B\).
nodes.statement_short: Each edge of $G^*$ is an edge of $G$ or a 2-path through $B$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Pull back the partition
nodes.statement:
For every edge $xy\in E(G^*)$, define \(f(xy) = \{xy\}\) if $x\in A'$ and $y\in B^*$,
and \(f(xy) = \{xv_{xy},v_{xy}y\}\) if \(x,y\in A'\). Note that $f(xy)\subset E(G)$ for every edge $xy\in E(G^*)$.
For a set \(S\subset E(G^*)\), put \(f(S) = \cup_{e\in S} f(e)\).
The partition of \(E(G^*)\) into \(M^*,F^*_1,\ldots,F^*_k\) induces 
a partition of \(E(G)\) into \(M = f(M^*)\) and \(F_i = f(F^*_i)\) for $1\leq i\leq k$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $f$ mapping edges of $G^*$ to edge sets of $G$; the partition pulls back.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement:
We will prove that \(\{M,F_1,\ldots,F_k\}\) is an \((A,1,2k+1)\)-fractional 
factorization. Fix $i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$. We will show that \(M\) is an \((A,1,2k+1)\)-factor of $G$ 
and \(F_i\) is an Eulerian \((A,2,2k+1)\)-factor of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $M$ is an $(A,1,2k+1)$-factor and each $F_i$ an Eulerian $(A,2,2k+1)$-factor.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Degree count
nodes.statement:
Let \(v\) be a vertex of \(A\) in \(G\) and put \(d'(v) = d(v)/(2k+1)\). Then, we know that 
\(v\) is represented by \(d'(v)\) vertices in \(G^*\).
Since \(M^*\) is a perfect matching in \(G^*\), there are \(d'(v)\) edges
of \(M\) entering \(v\) and, since \(F^*_i\) is a \(2\)-factor in \(G^*\),
there are \(2d'(v)\) edges of \(F_i\) incident to \(v\).
Finally, since \(F^*_i\) is Eulerian, the set
\(F_i\) is Eulerian, concluding the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Each $v\in A$ has $d'(v)$ copies, giving degrees $d'(v)$ in $M$ and $2d'(v)$ in $F_i$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: G* is 2k-edge-connected
nodes.statement: \(G^*\) is \(2k\)-edge connected.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 4.4
nodes.statement:
Let \(Y \subset V(G^*)\).
Suppose there is at least one vertex \(x\) of \(A'\) in \(Y\)
and at least one vertex \(y\) of \(A'\) in \(V(G^*)-Y\).
Since there are at least \(2k\) edge-disjoint paths joining \(x\) to \(y\),
there are at least \(2k\) edges with vertices in both \(Y\) and 
\(V(G^*)-Y\).
Now, suppose that \(A'\subset Y\) (otherwise \(A'\subset V(G^*)-Y\) and
we take \(V(G^*)-Y\) instead of \(Y\)), and then \(V(G^*)-Y \subset B^*\).
Since \(B^*\) is an independent set, all edges with a vertex in \(V(G^*)-Y\) 
must have the other vertex in \(A'\).
Since every vertex in \(B^*\) has degree \(2k+1\), 
there are at least \(2k+1\) edges with vertices in both \(Y\) and \(V(G^*)-Y\).
nodes.statement_short: Cut argument: a cut separating two $A'$ vertices has $\ge 2k$ edges; otherwise one side lies in the independent set $B^*$ of degree-$(2k+1)$ vertices.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Cut separates A' vertices
nodes.statement:
Let \(Y \subset V(G^*)\).
Suppose there is at least one vertex \(x\) of \(A'\) in \(Y\)
and at least one vertex \(y\) of \(A'\) in \(V(G^*)-Y\).
Since there are at least \(2k\) edge-disjoint paths joining \(x\) to \(y\),
there are at least \(2k\) edges with vertices in both \(Y\) and 
\(V(G^*)-Y\).
nodes.statement_short: Then $2k$ edge-disjoint paths cross the cut.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: One side inside B*
nodes.statement:
Now, suppose that \(A'\subset Y\) (otherwise \(A'\subset V(G^*)-Y\) and
we take \(V(G^*)-Y\) instead of \(Y\)), and then \(V(G^*)-Y \subset B^*\).
Since \(B^*\) is an independent set, all edges with a vertex in \(V(G^*)-Y\) 
must have the other vertex in \(A'\).
Since every vertex in \(B^*\) has degree \(2k+1\), 
there are at least \(2k+1\) edges with vertices in both \(Y\) and \(V(G^*)-Y\).
nodes.statement_short: All crossing edges go to $A'$, at least $2k+1$ of them.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Existence of (A,2,2k+2)-fractional factorizations
nodes.statement:
Let \(k\) be a positive integer.
If $G=(A,B;E)$ is a $32k$-edge-connected bipartite 
graph such 
that $d_G(v)$ is divisible by $2k+2$ for every 
$v\in A$, then $G$ admits an \((A,2,2k+2)\)-fractional factorization.
assumptions:
$d_G(v)$ is divisible by $2k+2$ for every 
$v\in A$
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations
nodes.label: corollary:even-special-decomposition

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.5
nodes.statement:
Let \(k\) and \(G=(A,B;E)\) be as in the hypothesis.
We claim that \(G\) contains an \((A,1,2k+2)\)-factor \(F\) such that
\(G-F\) is \(2k\)-edge-connected (note that this implies that $d_{G-F}(v)$ is 
divisible by $2k+1$ for every $v\in A$).


Since $G$ is $32k=16k\lceil(2k+2)/(2k+1)\rceil$-edge-connected, 
by Lemma~\ref{lem:barat-part-3} (applied with parameters $2k+1$, $m=2k$ and $r=1$), 
the graph $G$ admits a 
decomposition into graphs \(G_k\) and \(G_r\) such that \(G_k\) is 
\(2k\)-edge-connected and \(d_{G_k}(v) = 
\big((2k+1)/(2k+2)\big)d_G(v)\), and \(d_{G_r}(v) = \big(1/(2k+2)\big)d_G(v)\) 
for every \(v\in A\).
Therefore, \(E(G_r)\) is an \((A,1,2k+2)\)-factor.

By Lemma~\ref{lemma:1-special-decomposition}, \(G_k\) admits an 
\((A,1,2k+1)\)-fractional factorization 
\(\mathcal{F}\). Therefore, since \(d_{G_k}(v) = 
\big((2k+1)/(2k+2)\big)d_G(v)\) for every $v\in A$, we conclude that 
\(\mathcal{F} + E(G_r)\) is an 
\((A,2,2k+2)\)-fractional factorization of \(G\).
nodes.statement_short: Split off an $(A,1,2k+2)$-factor with Lemma 2.10 leaving a $2k$-edge-connected graph, then apply Lemma 4.3 to the rest.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Goal: split off a factor
nodes.statement:
Let \(k\) and \(G=(A,B;E)\) be as in the hypothesis.
We claim that \(G\) contains an \((A,1,2k+2)\)-factor \(F\) such that
\(G-F\) is \(2k\)-edge-connected (note that this implies that $d_{G-F}(v)$ is 
divisible by $2k+1$ for every $v\in A$).
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to find an $(A,1,2k+2)$-factor whose complement is $2k$-edge-connected.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 2.10
nodes.statement:
Since $G$ is $32k=16k\lceil(2k+2)/(2k+1)\rceil$-edge-connected, 
by Lemma~\ref{lem:barat-part-3} (applied with parameters $2k+1$, $m=2k$ and $r=1$), 
the graph $G$ admits a 
decomposition into graphs \(G_k\) and \(G_r\) such that \(G_k\) is 
\(2k\)-edge-connected and \(d_{G_k}(v) = 
\big((2k+1)/(2k+2)\big)d_G(v)\), and \(d_{G_r}(v) = \big(1/(2k+2)\big)d_G(v)\) 
for every \(v\in A\).
Therefore, \(E(G_r)\) is an \((A,1,2k+2)\)-factor.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2.10 with $m=2k$, $r=1$ splits $G$ into $G_k$ and the factor $G_r$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 4.3
nodes.statement:
By Lemma~\ref{lemma:1-special-decomposition}, \(G_k\) admits an 
\((A,1,2k+1)\)-fractional factorization 
\(\mathcal{F}\). Therefore, since \(d_{G_k}(v) = 
\big((2k+1)/(2k+2)\big)d_G(v)\) for every $v\in A$, we conclude that 
\(\mathcal{F} + E(G_r)\) is an 
\((A,2,2k+2)\)-fractional factorization of \(G\).
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 4.3 on $G_k$ plus $E(G_r)$ gives the fractional factorization.
nodes.section: 4.1 Fractional factorizations

nodes.name: (l,k)-bifactorization
nodes.statement:
Let \(k\) and \(\ell\) be positive integers such that $k-\ell$ is a positive 
even number, and let \(G=(A_1,A_2;E)\) be a bipartite graph. 

Let \(\mathcal{F}_1,\mathcal{F}_2\) be families of subsets of \(E\)
and put \(G_i = G[\cup_{F\in\mathcal{F}_i}F]\), for \(i=1,2\).
We say that \(\mathbb{F}=(\mathcal{F}_1,\mathcal{F}_2)\) is an 
\emph{\((\ell,k)\)-bifactorization of \(G\)}
if the following holds.
\begin{itemize}
 \item [(i)] \(\{G_1,G_2\}\) is a decomposition of \(G\) ;
 \item [(ii)] \(\mathcal{F}_i\) is an \((A_i,\ell,k)\)-fractional 
factorization of $G_i$, for $1\leq i\leq 2$.
\end{itemize}



If \(G\) admits an \((\ell,k)\)-bifactorization,
we say that \(G\) is \((\ell,k)\)-bifactorable.
nodes.statement_short: A split of a bipartite graph into $G_1,G_2$ with an $(A_i,\ell,k)$-fractional factorization of each $G_i$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Bifactorizations
nodes.label: def:bip-factor

nodes.name: Strong bifactorization
nodes.statement:
Let \(k\) and \(\ell\) be positive integers.
Let \(G = (A_1,A_2;E)\) be a bipartite graph that admits an
\((\ell,k)\)-bifactorization \(\mathbb{F} = (\mathcal{F}_1,\mathcal{F}_2)\).
Let \(E_i = \bigcup_{F\in\mathcal{F}_i} F\) for $1\leq i\leq 2$. 
Let $p=1$ if $\ell$ is odd, and $p=2$ if $\ell$ is even. 
We say that \(\mathbb{F}\) is \emph{strong}
if \(d_{E_i}(v)\geq (k/p)((k/p)+p)\) for every 
\(v\) in \(A_i\)
for $1\leq i\leq 2$.



If \(G\) admits a strong \((\ell,k)\)-bifactorization, we say that \(G\) is 
\emph{strongly \((\ell,k)\)-bifactorable}.
nodes.section: 4.2 Bifactorizations

nodes.name: Element of a bifactorization
nodes.statement:
For ease of notation, if \(F\) belongs to either \(\mathcal{F}_1\) or 
\(\mathcal{F}_2\), then
we say that \(F\) is an element of \(\mathbb{F}\).
nodes.section: 4.2 Bifactorizations

nodes.name: Strong (1,2k+1)-bifactorability of highly edge-connected bipartite graphs
nodes.statement:
Let \(k\) be a positive integer. Let \(r = (2k+1)(2k+2)\).
	If \(G\) is a  \(2(6k + 2r+1)\)-edge-connected 
	bipartite graph such that \(|E(G)|\) is divisible by \(2k+1\),
	then \(G\) is strongly \((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorable.
assumptions: Let \(k\) be a positive integer. Let \(r = (2k+1)(2k+2)\).
nodes.section: 4.2 Bifactorizations
nodes.label: lemma:odd-strong-factorization

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.8
nodes.statement:
Let $k$, $r$ and $G=(A,B;E)$ be as in the hypothesis.
	By Lemma~\ref{lem:tight-good-initial-decomposition} (applied with 
\(2k+1\) and $r$), the graph \(G\) can be decomposed into two spanning edge-disjoint 
\(r\)-edge-connected 
	graphs \(G_1\) and \(G_2\) such that all vertices of \(A\) have degree 
divisible by \(2k+1\)
	in \(G_1\), and all vertices of \(B\) have degree divisible by 
\(2k+1\) 
in \(G_2\).  But since $r\geq 2k$, by Lemma~\ref{lemma:1-special-decomposition} (applied with \(k\)), 
	we conclude that \(G_1\) admits 
	an \((A,1,2k+1)\)-fractional factorization
	and \(G_2\) admits a \((B,1,2k+1)\)-fractional factorization.
	Therefore, \(G\) is \((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorable.

	Since \(G_1\) and \(G_2\) are \(r\)-edge-connected,
	we have \(d_{G_1}(v) \geq (2k+1)(2k+2)\) for every \(v\in A\),
	and \(d_{G_2}(v) \geq (2k+1)(2k+2)\) for every \(v\in B\), from 
where we conclude that \(G\) is strongly 
\((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorable.
nodes.statement_short: Split $G$ by Lemma 2.5 into two $r$-edge-connected parts and apply Lemma 4.3 to each; $r$-edge-connectivity gives the strong degree bound.
nodes.section: 4.2 Bifactorizations

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 2.5
nodes.statement:
Let $k$, $r$ and $G=(A,B;E)$ be as in the hypothesis.
	By Lemma~\ref{lem:tight-good-initial-decomposition} (applied with 
\(2k+1\) and $r$), the graph \(G\) can be decomposed into two spanning edge-disjoint 
\(r\)-edge-connected 
	graphs \(G_1\) and \(G_2\) such that all vertices of \(A\) have degree 
divisible by \(2k+1\)
	in \(G_1\), and all vertices of \(B\) have degree divisible by 
\(2k+1\) 
in \(G_2\).
nodes.statement_short: Decompose $G$ into $r$-edge-connected $G_1,G_2$ with divisible degrees.
nodes.section: 4.2 Bifactorizations

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 4.3
nodes.statement:
But since $r\geq 2k$, by Lemma~\ref{lemma:1-special-decomposition} (applied with \(k\)), 
	we conclude that \(G_1\) admits 
	an \((A,1,2k+1)\)-fractional factorization
	and \(G_2\) admits a \((B,1,2k+1)\)-fractional factorization.
	Therefore, \(G\) is \((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorable.
nodes.statement_short: Each $G_i$ has a fractional factorization, so $G$ is bifactorable.
nodes.section: 4.2 Bifactorizations

nodes.name: Strongness
nodes.statement:
Since \(G_1\) and \(G_2\) are \(r\)-edge-connected,
	we have \(d_{G_1}(v) \geq (2k+1)(2k+2)\) for every \(v\in A\),
	and \(d_{G_2}(v) \geq (2k+1)(2k+2)\) for every \(v\in B\), from 
where we conclude that \(G\) is strongly 
\((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorable.
nodes.statement_short: Minimum degree at least $r$ gives the strong bound.
nodes.section: 4.2 Bifactorizations

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.9 (sketch)
nodes.statement:
The proof of the next lemma can be easily obtained by replacing Lemma~\ref{lemma:1-special-decomposition} with
Corollary~\ref{corollary:even-special-decomposition} in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma:odd-strong-factorization}.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat the proof of Lemma 4.8 with Corollary 4.5 in place of Lemma 4.3.
nodes.section: 4.2 Bifactorizations

nodes.name: Strong (2,2k+2)-bifactorability of highly edge-connected bipartite graphs
nodes.statement:
Let \(k\) be a positive integer.
	Let \(r = \max\{32k,(k+1)(k+3)\}\).
	If \(G\) is a  \(2(6k + 2r + 4)\)-edge-connected bipartite graph
	 such that \(|E(G)|\) is divisible by \(2k+2\),
	then \(G\) is strongly \((2,2k+2)\)-bifactorable.
nodes.section: 4.2 Bifactorizations
nodes.label: lemma:even-strong-factorization

nodes.name: F-balanced tracking decomposition (odd case)
nodes.statement:
Let \(k\) be a positive integer.
Let \(G = (A,B;E)\) be a bipartite graph 
that admits a \((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorization 
\(\mathbb{F}=(\mathcal{F}_1,\mathcal{F}_2)\),
and let \(G_i = G\big[\bigcup_{F\in\mathcal{F}_i}F\big]\) for \(i=1,2\).
Let \(M_1\) be the \((A,1,2k+1)\)-factor of \(\mathbb{F}\) and \(M_2\) be the
\((B,1,2k+1)\)-factor of \(\mathbb{F}\).

We say that 
a \((2k+1)\)-tracking decomposition \(\mathcal{B}\) of \(G\) is \emph{\(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced}

if the following holds.
	\begin{itemize}
		\item \(\mathcal{B}(v) = d_{G_1}(v)/(2k+1) + d_{M_2}(v)\) for every \(v\in A\);
		\item \(\mathcal{B}(v) = d_{G_2}(v)/(2k+1) + d_{M_1}(v)\) for every \(v\in B\).
	\end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: A $(2k+1)$-tracking decomposition whose end-counts are $d_{G_1}(v)/(2k+1)+d_{M_2}(v)$ on $A$ and symmetrically on $B$.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Balanced 3-path decomposition from a (1,3)-bifactorization
nodes.statement:
Let \(G\) be a bipartite graph that admits a 
	\((1,3)\)-bifactorization \(\mathbb{F}\).
	Then \(G\) admits an \(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced $3$-path tracking decomposition.
assumptions:
Let \(G\) be a bipartite graph that admits a 
	\((1,3)\)-bifactorization \(\mathbb{F}\)
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length
nodes.label: lemma:3-PD

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.2
nodes.statement:
Let \(G = (A,B;E)\) be a bipartite graph that admits a 
	\((1,3)\)-bifactorization \(\mathbb{F}= (\mathcal{F}_1,\mathcal{F}_2)\) 
and put \(\mathcal{F}_i = \{M_i,F_i\}\) for \(i = 1,2\).






	Let \(\mathcal{C}_1\) be the set of components of \(G[F_1]\).
	Let \(T\) be an element of \(\mathcal{C}_1\)
	and \(B_T = a_0b_0a_1b_1\cdots a_sb_sa_0\) be a tracking of \(T\),
	where \(a_i \in A\) and \(b_i \in B\), for \(1\leq i\leq s\).
	We have that \(\mathcal{B}'_T = \{a_ib_ia_{i+1}\colon 0\leq i\leq s\}\), taking \(a_{s+1} = a_0\),
	is a \(2\)-tracking decomposition of \(T\)
	in which every tracking has its end-vertices in \(A\).
	Therefore, \(\mathcal{B}'_1 = \cup_{T \in \mathcal{C}_1}  \mathcal{B}'_T\)
	is a \(2\)-tracking decomposition of \(G[F_1]\)
	in which every tracking has its end-vertices in \(A\).




	Analogously, \(G[F_2]\) admits a \(2\)-tracking decomposition \(\mathcal{B}'_2\)
	in which every tracking has its end-vertices in \(B\).






	
	Let \(G_i = G[M_i\cup F_i]\) for \(i = 1,2\).
	Note that, since \(M_1\) is an \((A,1,3)\)-factor and \(F_1\) is an 
\((A,2,3)\)-factor
	of \(G_1\), we have \(d_{F_1}(v) = (2/3)d_{G_1}(v) = 2d_{M_1}(v)\),
	for every vertex \(v\) in \(A\).
	Note that the number of trackings in \(\mathcal{B}'_1\) that end at a vertex \(v\) 
	equals \(\frac{1}{2}d_{F_1}(v) = d_{M_1}(v)\).






	Thus, we can extend each tracking \(B\) of \(\mathcal{B}'_1\) by adding 
	an edge of \(M_1\) to the start vertex of \(B\),
	obtaining a \(3\)-path tracking decomposition \(\mathcal{B}_1\) of \(G_1\).
	Analogously, we can extend each tracking \(T\) of \(\mathcal{B}'_2\) by adding
	an edge of \(M_2\) to the starting vertex of \(T\),
	obtaining a \(3\)-path tracking decomposition \(\mathcal{B}_2\) of \(G_2\).
	
	
	Put \(\mathcal{B} = \mathcal{B}_1\cup\mathcal{B}_2\). 
	If \(v\) is a vertex of \(A\), then the number of paths having \(v\) as end-vertex
	is exactly \(d_{F_1}(v)/2 + d_{M_2}(v)\).

	Therefore,
	we have \(\mathcal{B}(v) =  d_{F_1}(v)/2 +  d_{M_2}(v)  = d_{G_1}(v)/3 + d_{M_2}(v)\).
	Analogously, we have \(\mathcal{B}(v) = d_{G_2}(v)/3 + d_{M_1}(v)\)
	for every vertex \(v\) in \(B\).
	Thus, \(\mathcal{B}\) is an \(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced $3$-path tracking decomposition of \(G\).
nodes.statement_short: Split Eulerian 2-factors into 2-paths ending in $A$ (resp. $B$) and extend each by a matching edge to get 3-paths with the right end-counts.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: 2-tracking decomposition of G[F_1]
nodes.statement:
Let \(G = (A,B;E)\) be a bipartite graph that admits a 
	\((1,3)\)-bifactorization \(\mathbb{F}= (\mathcal{F}_1,\mathcal{F}_2)\) 
and put \(\mathcal{F}_i = \{M_i,F_i\}\) for \(i = 1,2\).






	Let \(\mathcal{C}_1\) be the set of components of \(G[F_1]\).
	Let \(T\) be an element of \(\mathcal{C}_1\)
	and \(B_T = a_0b_0a_1b_1\cdots a_sb_sa_0\) be a tracking of \(T\),
	where \(a_i \in A\) and \(b_i \in B\), for \(1\leq i\leq s\).
	We have that \(\mathcal{B}'_T = \{a_ib_ia_{i+1}\colon 0\leq i\leq s\}\), taking \(a_{s+1} = a_0\),
	is a \(2\)-tracking decomposition of \(T\)
	in which every tracking has its end-vertices in \(A\).
	Therefore, \(\mathcal{B}'_1 = \cup_{T \in \mathcal{C}_1}  \mathcal{B}'_T\)
	is a \(2\)-tracking decomposition of \(G[F_1]\)
	in which every tracking has its end-vertices in \(A\).
nodes.statement_short: Cut each closed tracking of a component of $G[F_1]$ into 2-trackings with ends in $A$.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Same for G[F_2]
nodes.statement:
Analogously, \(G[F_2]\) admits a \(2\)-tracking decomposition \(\mathcal{B}'_2\)
	in which every tracking has its end-vertices in \(B\).
nodes.statement_short: Symmetrically for $G[F_2]$ with ends in $B$.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Count ends
nodes.statement:
Let \(G_i = G[M_i\cup F_i]\) for \(i = 1,2\).
	Note that, since \(M_1\) is an \((A,1,3)\)-factor and \(F_1\) is an 
\((A,2,3)\)-factor
	of \(G_1\), we have \(d_{F_1}(v) = (2/3)d_{G_1}(v) = 2d_{M_1}(v)\),
	for every vertex \(v\) in \(A\).
	Note that the number of trackings in \(\mathcal{B}'_1\) that end at a vertex \(v\) 
	equals \(\frac{1}{2}d_{F_1}(v) = d_{M_1}(v)\).
nodes.statement_short: The number of 2-trackings ending at $v\in A$ equals $d_{M_1}(v)$.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Extend by matching edges
nodes.statement:
Thus, we can extend each tracking \(B\) of \(\mathcal{B}'_1\) by adding 
	an edge of \(M_1\) to the start vertex of \(B\),
	obtaining a \(3\)-path tracking decomposition \(\mathcal{B}_1\) of \(G_1\).
	Analogously, we can extend each tracking \(T\) of \(\mathcal{B}'_2\) by adding
	an edge of \(M_2\) to the starting vertex of \(T\),
	obtaining a \(3\)-path tracking decomposition \(\mathcal{B}_2\) of \(G_2\).
nodes.statement_short: Add an $M_i$ edge to each 2-tracking to get 3-path decompositions.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Balanced
nodes.statement:
Put \(\mathcal{B} = \mathcal{B}_1\cup\mathcal{B}_2\). 
	If \(v\) is a vertex of \(A\), then the number of paths having \(v\) as end-vertex
	is exactly \(d_{F_1}(v)/2 + d_{M_2}(v)\).

	Therefore,
	we have \(\mathcal{B}(v) =  d_{F_1}(v)/2 +  d_{M_2}(v)  = d_{G_1}(v)/3 + d_{M_2}(v)\).
	Analogously, we have \(\mathcal{B}(v) = d_{G_2}(v)/3 + d_{M_1}(v)\)
	for every vertex \(v\) in \(B\).
	Thus, \(\mathcal{B}\) is an \(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced $3$-path tracking decomposition of \(G\).
nodes.statement_short: Count path ends at each vertex to verify $\mathbb{F}$-balance.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Pre-completeness gives completeness (odd case)
nodes.statement:
Let \(k\) be a positive integer and let 
	\(G\) be a bipartite graph that admits a  
	\((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorization \(\mathbb{F}\).
	If \(G\) admits an \(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced 
\((2k+1)\)-pre-complete
	$(2k+1)$-tracking decomposition, 
	then \(G\) admits an \(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced \((k+1)\)-complete 
	$(2k+1)$-tracking decomposition.
assumptions:
Let \(k\) be a positive integer and let 
	\(G\) be a bipartite graph that admits a  
	\((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorization \(\mathbb{F}\)
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length
nodes.label: lemma:odd-complete

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.3
nodes.statement:
Let \(k\) be a positive integer and let \(G = (A,B;E)\) be a bipartite 
graph that admits a 
	\((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorization \(\mathbb{F}\). Let
$\mathcal{F}$ be the set of all $\mathbb{F}$-balanced 
	\((2k+1)\)-pre-complete $(2k+1)$-tracking decompositions of $G$. 
	Now let $\mathcal{B}$ be a tracking decomposition in $\mathcal{F}$ such that \(\sum_{v\in V(G)} 
\mathrm{hang}(v,\mathcal{B})\) is maximum over all tracking decompositions in $\mathcal{F}$.
	We claim that \(\mathcal{B}\) is a \((k+1)\)-complete tracking decomposition,
	i.e,  \(\mathrm{hang}(v,\mathcal{B}) > k+1\) for each vertex \(v\) of~\(G\).

	Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(\mathcal{B}\) is not \((k+1)\)-complete.
	Then there is a vertex \(v\) of \(G\) such that \(\mathrm{hang}(v,\mathcal{B}) \leq k+1\).
	Suppose, without loss of generality, that \(v\) is a vertex of \(A\).
	Since \(\mathcal{B}\) is \((2k+1)\)-pre-complete, \(\mathrm{preHang}(v,\mathcal{B}) \geq 2k+2\).
	Thus, there are at least \(k+1\) pre-hanging edges at \(v\) 
	that are not hanging edges at \(v\), say \(x_1v,\ldots,x_{k+1}v\).
	Let \(T_1 = y_0y_1\cdots y_{2k+1}\) be the element of \(\mathcal{B}\) that contains \(x_1v\),
	where, without loss of generality, \(y_0 = x_1\) and \(y_1 = v\).
	The vertices of \(T_1\) in \(B\) are \(y_0,y_2,\ldots, y_{2k}\). 
	First, we will show that $x_i\notin V(T_1)$ for some \(2\leq i \leq k+1\). 

	Since \(y_2\) is in \(B\) and \(y_0\) is the end-vertex of \(T_1\) in 
\(B\),
	the vertex \(y_2\) is not an end-vertex of \(T_1\). 
	Since \(y_1y_2 \in E(T_1)\), the edge \(y_1y_2\) is not a pre-hanging 
edge at \(v\).
	Then, \(y_2 \neq x_i\) for every \(2\leq i\leq k+1\).
	Therefore, \(|\{y_4, y_6,\ldots,y_{2k}\}| = k-1\) and 
\(|\{x_2,\ldots,x_{k+1}\}| = k\), from where we conclude that
	for at least one \(i\), we have \(x_i \notin V(T_1)\).
	
	Now let \(T_i = z_0z_1\cdots z_{2k+1}\) be the element of \(\mathcal{B}\) that contains \(x_iv\).
	Suppose, without loss of generality, that \(z_1 = v\) and \(z_0 = x_i\).
	Let \(T'_1 = vy_1\cdots y_{2k+1}\) and \(T'_i = y_0z_1\cdots z_{2k+1}\),
	and let \(\mathcal{B}' = \mathcal{B} - T_1 - T_i + T'_1 + T'_i\).
	We note that \(\bar T'_1 = \bar T_1 - x_1v + x_iv\) 
	and \(\bar T'_i = \bar T_i -x_iv + x_1v\).
	Since \(x_i \notin V(T_1)\), we have \(d_{T'_1}(x_i) = 1\), which 
	implies that \(x_iv\) is a hanging edge of \(\mathcal{B}'\) at~$v$. Therefore, 
	\(\sum_{v\in V(G)} \mathrm{hang}(v,\mathcal{B}') > \sum_{v\in V(G)} \mathrm{hang}(v,\mathcal{B})\).

	We claim that \(\mathcal{B}'\) is \(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced.
	Indeed, since the set of pre-hanging edges at \(v\) is the same in \(\mathcal{B}\) 
	and \(\mathcal{B}'\), we have \(\mathcal{B}(v) = \mathcal{B}'(v)\) for every \(v\) in \(V(G)\).
	Therefore, \(\mathcal{B}'\) is an \hbox{\(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced} \((2k+1)\)-pre-complete
	tracking decomposition such that 
	\(\sum_{v\in V(G)} \mathrm{hang}(v,\mathcal{B}') > \sum_{v\in V(G)} \mathrm{hang}(v,\mathcal{B})\),	
	a contradiction to the choice of \(\mathcal{B}\).
nodes.statement_short: Extremal choice: take a balanced pre-complete decomposition maximizing the number of hanging edges; a vertex with too few hanging edges allows an edge swap that increases it.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Extremal decomposition
nodes.statement:
Let \(k\) be a positive integer and let \(G = (A,B;E)\) be a bipartite 
graph that admits a 
	\((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorization \(\mathbb{F}\). Let
$\mathcal{F}$ be the set of all $\mathbb{F}$-balanced 
	\((2k+1)\)-pre-complete $(2k+1)$-tracking decompositions of $G$. 
	Now let $\mathcal{B}$ be a tracking decomposition in $\mathcal{F}$ such that \(\sum_{v\in V(G)} 
\mathrm{hang}(v,\mathcal{B})\) is maximum over all tracking decompositions in $\mathcal{F}$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\mathcal{B}$ maximizing the total number of hanging edges.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Claim completeness
nodes.statement:
We claim that \(\mathcal{B}\) is a \((k+1)\)-complete tracking decomposition,
	i.e,  \(\mathrm{hang}(v,\mathcal{B}) > k+1\) for each vertex \(v\) of~\(G\).
nodes.statement_short: Claim: $\mathcal{B}$ is $(k+1)$-complete.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Bad vertex
nodes.statement:
Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(\mathcal{B}\) is not \((k+1)\)-complete.
	Then there is a vertex \(v\) of \(G\) such that \(\mathrm{hang}(v,\mathcal{B}) \leq k+1\).
	Suppose, without loss of generality, that \(v\) is a vertex of \(A\).
	Since \(\mathcal{B}\) is \((2k+1)\)-pre-complete, \(\mathrm{preHang}(v,\mathcal{B}) \geq 2k+2\).
	Thus, there are at least \(k+1\) pre-hanging edges at \(v\) 
	that are not hanging edges at \(v\), say \(x_1v,\ldots,x_{k+1}v\).
	Let \(T_1 = y_0y_1\cdots y_{2k+1}\) be the element of \(\mathcal{B}\) that contains \(x_1v\),
	where, without loss of generality, \(y_0 = x_1\) and \(y_1 = v\).
	The vertices of \(T_1\) in \(B\) are \(y_0,y_2,\ldots, y_{2k}\). 
	First, we will show that $x_i\notin V(T_1)$ for some \(2\leq i \leq k+1\).
nodes.statement_short: Take $v\in A$ with few hanging edges; pre-completeness gives many non-hanging pre-hanging edges $x_iv$.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Find x_i outside T_1
nodes.statement:
Since \(y_2\) is in \(B\) and \(y_0\) is the end-vertex of \(T_1\) in 
\(B\),
	the vertex \(y_2\) is not an end-vertex of \(T_1\). 
	Since \(y_1y_2 \in E(T_1)\), the edge \(y_1y_2\) is not a pre-hanging 
edge at \(v\).
	Then, \(y_2 \neq x_i\) for every \(2\leq i\leq k+1\).
	Therefore, \(|\{y_4, y_6,\ldots,y_{2k}\}| = k-1\) and 
\(|\{x_2,\ldots,x_{k+1}\}| = k\), from where we conclude that
	for at least one \(i\), we have \(x_i \notin V(T_1)\).
nodes.statement_short: Counting the $B$-vertices of $T_1$ shows some $x_i\notin V(T_1)$.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Swap edges
nodes.statement:
Now let \(T_i = z_0z_1\cdots z_{2k+1}\) be the element of \(\mathcal{B}\) that contains \(x_iv\).
	Suppose, without loss of generality, that \(z_1 = v\) and \(z_0 = x_i\).
	Let \(T'_1 = vy_1\cdots y_{2k+1}\) and \(T'_i = y_0z_1\cdots z_{2k+1}\),
	and let \(\mathcal{B}' = \mathcal{B} - T_1 - T_i + T'_1 + T'_i\).
	We note that \(\bar T'_1 = \bar T_1 - x_1v + x_iv\) 
	and \(\bar T'_i = \bar T_i -x_iv + x_1v\).
	Since \(x_i \notin V(T_1)\), we have \(d_{T'_1}(x_i) = 1\), which 
	implies that \(x_iv\) is a hanging edge of \(\mathcal{B}'\) at~$v$. Therefore, 
	\(\sum_{v\in V(G)} \mathrm{hang}(v,\mathcal{B}') > \sum_{v\in V(G)} \mathrm{hang}(v,\mathcal{B})\).
nodes.statement_short: Exchange $x_1v$ and $x_iv$ between $T_1$ and $T_i$, creating a new hanging edge.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Balance preserved; contradiction
nodes.statement:
We claim that \(\mathcal{B}'\) is \(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced.
	Indeed, since the set of pre-hanging edges at \(v\) is the same in \(\mathcal{B}\) 
	and \(\mathcal{B}'\), we have \(\mathcal{B}(v) = \mathcal{B}'(v)\) for every \(v\) in \(V(G)\).
	Therefore, \(\mathcal{B}'\) is an \hbox{\(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced} \((2k+1)\)-pre-complete
	tracking decomposition such that 
	\(\sum_{v\in V(G)} \mathrm{hang}(v,\mathcal{B}') > \sum_{v\in V(G)} \mathrm{hang}(v,\mathcal{B})\),	
	a contradiction to the choice of \(\mathcal{B}\).
nodes.statement_short: Pre-hanging edges are unchanged, so $\mathcal{B}'$ is balanced, contradicting maximality.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: End-counts unchanged
nodes.statement:
Indeed, since the set of pre-hanging edges at \(v\) is the same in \(\mathcal{B}\) 
	and \(\mathcal{B}'\), we have \(\mathcal{B}(v) = \mathcal{B}'(v)\) for every \(v\) in \(V(G)\).
nodes.statement_short: Pre-hanging edges are the same, so $\mathcal{B}'(v)=\mathcal{B}(v)$.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement:
Therefore, \(\mathcal{B}'\) is an \hbox{\(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced} \((2k+1)\)-pre-complete
	tracking decomposition such that 
	\(\sum_{v\in V(G)} \mathrm{hang}(v,\mathcal{B}') > \sum_{v\in V(G)} \mathrm{hang}(v,\mathcal{B})\),	
	a contradiction to the choice of \(\mathcal{B}\).
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{B}'$ has more hanging edges, contradicting the choice of $\mathcal{B}$.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Balanced complete path decomposition via disentangling (odd case)
nodes.statement:
Let \(k\) be a positive integer and let \(G\) be a bipartite graph that 
admits a 
	\((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorization \(\mathbb{F}\).
	If \(G\) admits an \(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced \((k+1)\)-complete 
	$(2k+1)$-tracking decomposition, 
	then \(G\) admits an \(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced \((k+1)\)-complete 
	$(2k+1)$-path tracking decomposition.
assumptions:
Let \(k\) be a positive integer and let \(G\) be a bipartite graph that 
admits a 
	\((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorization \(\mathbb{F}\)
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length
nodes.label: lemma:odd-path-dec

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.4
nodes.statement:
Let \(k\) be a positive integer and let \(G = (A,B;E)\) be a bipartite 
graph that admits a \((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorization \(\mathbb{F}\).
	Suppose \(G\) admits an \(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced 
\((k+1)\)-complete
	$(2k+1)$-tracking decomposition \(\mathcal{B}\).
	By Lemma~\ref{lemma:disentangling} (applied with \(\ell = 2k+1\)),
	the graph \(G\) admits a \((k+1)\)-complete \((2k+1)\)-path tracking decomposition \(\mathcal{B}'\)
	
	such that \(\mathcal{B}'(v) = \mathcal{B}(v)\) for every vertex \(v\) of \(G\). 
	Therefore, \(\mathcal{B}'\) is an \(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced 
	\((k+1)\)-complete $(2k+1)$-path tracking decomposition.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Disentangling Lemma with $\ell=2k+1$; it preserves end-counts and hence balance.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Set up
nodes.statement:
Let \(k\) be a positive integer and let \(G = (A,B;E)\) be a bipartite 
graph that admits a \((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorization \(\mathbb{F}\).
	Suppose \(G\) admits an \(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced 
\((k+1)\)-complete
	$(2k+1)$-tracking decomposition \(\mathcal{B}\).
nodes.statement_short: Fix the balanced $(k+1)$-complete tracking decomposition $\mathcal{B}$.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Disentangle
nodes.statement:
By Lemma~\ref{lemma:disentangling} (applied with \(\ell = 2k+1\)),
	the graph \(G\) admits a \((k+1)\)-complete \((2k+1)\)-path tracking decomposition \(\mathcal{B}'\)
	
	such that \(\mathcal{B}'(v) = \mathcal{B}(v)\) for every vertex \(v\) of \(G\). 
	Therefore, \(\mathcal{B}'\) is an \(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced 
	\((k+1)\)-complete $(2k+1)$-path tracking decomposition.
nodes.statement_short: The Disentangling Lemma gives a path decomposition with the same end-counts, hence balanced.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Balanced odd path decomposition from a strong bifactorization
nodes.statement:
Let \(k\) be a positive integer. If \(G\) is a bipartite graph that 
admits a strong  \((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorization \(\mathbb{F}\),
	then \(G\) admits an \(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced $(2k+1)$-path tracking decomposition.
assumptions:
\(G\) is a bipartite graph that 
admits a strong  \((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorization \(\mathbb{F}\)
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length
nodes.label: thm:odd-path-decomposition

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.5
nodes.statement:
The proof is by induction on \(k\).
By Lemma~\ref{lemma:3-PD}, the statement is true for \(k=1\).
Thus, suppose \(k>1\),
and let \(G = (A_1,A_2;E)\) be a bipartite graph that admits a strong  
\((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorization \(\mathbb{F} = (\mathcal{F}_1,\mathcal{F}_2)\).
We claim that \(G\) admits an \(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced 
\((2k+1)\)-pre-complete 
$(2k+1)$-tracking decomposition.
Let \(\mathcal{F}_1 = \{M_1,F_{1,1},\ldots,F_{1,k}\}\) 
and \(\mathcal{F}_2 = \{M_2,F_{2,2},\ldots,F_{2,k}\}\),
and let \(G_i = G\big[\bigcup_{F\in\mathcal{F}_i} F\big]\) for \(i = 1,2\).
Hereafter, fix $i \in \{1,2\}$.

Define \(d^*(v) = 
d_{G_i}(v)/(2k+1)\) for every vertex \(v\) in \(A_i\).
Note that \(d_{F_{i,j}}(v) = 2d^*(v) = 2d_{M_i}(v)\) for every vertex \(v\) in 
\(A_i\) and \(1\leq j\leq k\). 
Let \(O_{F_{i,k}}\) be a Eulerian 
orientation of \(F_{i,k}\).
Let \(F_{i,k} = F_{i,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits} \cup F_{i,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}\), where 
\(F_{i,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}\) is the set of 
edges
of \(F_{i,k}\) leaving \(A_i\) in \(O_{F_{i,k}}\),
and \(F_{i,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}\) is the set of edges of \(F_{i,k}\) entering
\(A_i\)
in \(O_{F_{i,k}}\).
Note that, since \(O_{F_{i,k}}\) is an Eulerian orientation,
\(d_{F_{i,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(v) = d_{F_{i,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}}(v) = d_{F_{i,k}}(v)/2\) for 
every 
vertex \(v\in A_i\).

Let \(G' = G - M_1 - M_2 - F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits} - F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}\),
and define \(\mathcal{F}'_i = \{F_{i,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits},F_{i,1},\ldots, F_{i,k-1}\}\).
Let \(G'_i = G\big[\bigcup_{F\in\mathcal{F}'_i} F\big]\).
Note that \(G'_i = G_i - M_i - F_{i,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}\).
Then, for every vertex \(v\in A_i\), we have
\begin{equation} d_{G'_i}(v) = d_{G_i}(v) - 2d^*(v) 
	    = (2k+1)d^*(v) - 2d^*(v) 
	    = (2k-1)d^*(v).
\end{equation}

\begin{claim}
\(\mathbb{F}' = (\mathcal{F}'_1,\mathcal{F}'_2)\) is a strong 
\((1,2k-1)\)-bifactorization of \(G'\).
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}

To prove this claim, we shall prove the following.
\begin{itemize}
	\item[(i)] \(F_{i,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}\) is an \((A_i,1,2k-1)\)-factor of 
\(G'_i\);
	\item[(ii)] \(F_{i,j}\) is an Eulerian \((A_i,2,2k-1)\)-factor 
			of \(G'_i\) for \(1\leq j\leq k-1\);
	\item[(iii)] \(d_{G'_i}(v) \geq (2k-1)(2k)\) for every vertex \(v\in 
A_i\).
\end{itemize}

To prove items (i) and (ii), first 
note that, for every $v\in A_i$, we have \(d_{F_{i,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}}(v) = 
d^*(v)\) and \(d_{F_{i,j}}(v) = 2d^*(v)\) for every \(1\leq 
j\leq k-1\). By~\eqref{odd-d}, we conclude that \(F_{i,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}\) is a 
\((A_i,1,2k-1)\)-factor of 
\(G'_i\) and \(F_{i,j}\) is an \((A_i,2,2k-1)\)-factor of \(G'_i\). 
Since \(\mathbb{F}\) is a \((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorization,
\(F_{1,j}\) and \(F_{2,j}\) are Eulerian graphs for 
\(1\leq j\leq k-1\).

It remains to prove item (iii).
Since \(d_{G'_i}(v) = (2k-1)d^*(v)\) and \(d^*(v) = d_{G_i}(v)/(2k+1)\) for 
every vertex \(v\in A_i\),
we have \(d_{G'_i}(v) = \frac{2k-1}{2k+1}d_{G_i}(v)\) for every \(v\in A_i\).
Since \(\mathbb{F}\) is a strong \((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorization, 
\(d_{G_i}(v) \geq (2k+1)(2k+2)\) for every \(v\in A_i\).
Therefore, \(d_{G'_i}(v) \geq (2k-1)(2k+2) > (2k-1)2k\) for every \(v\in 
A_i\).
\end{proof}

Since 
\(\mathbb{F}'\) is a strong \((1,2k-1)\)-bifactorization of \(G'\),
by the induction hypothesis, 
\(G'\) admits an \(\mathbb{F}'\)-balanced $(2k-1)$-path 
tracking decomposition \(\mathcal{B}'\).

Since \(\mathcal{B}'\) is a \(\mathbb{F}'\)-balanced $(2k-1)$-path tracking decomposition, we have
	\begin{itemize}
		\item \(\mathcal{B}'(v) = d_{G'_1}(v)/(2k-1) + d_{F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}}(v)\) 
for every 
\(v\in A_1\);
		\item \(\mathcal{B}'(v) = d_{G'_2}(v)/(2k-1) + d_{F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}}(v)\) 
for every 
\(v\in A_2\).
	\end{itemize}


Now we want to extend each tracking in \(\mathcal{B}'\) to obtain 

a \((2k+1)\)-tracking decomposition of \(G\).
For that, we add edges from  
\(E(G) - E(G')\) at the end-vertices of the trackings in $\mathcal{B}'$.
For each \(v\in A_1\) (\(v\in A_2\)), let \(S_v\) be the set of edges of 
\(M_1\cup F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}\) (\(M_2\cup F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}\)) that are incident 
to \(v\).
Note that for each edge \(e\) in \(E(G) - E(G')\) 
there is exactly one \(v\in V(G)\) such that \(e\in S_v\).
Then, \(\bigcup_{v\in V(G)} S_v = E(G) - 
E(G')\).
Therefore, if we prove that \(\mathcal{B}'(v) = |S_v|\), then we can extend every 
tracking $B$ in $\mathcal{B}'$ by adding one edge at each end-vertex of $B$.


\begin{claim}
	\(\mathcal{B}'(v) = |S_v|\), for every $v\in V(G)$.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
First, note that, since \(F_{i,k}\) is Eulerian, we have 
\(d_{F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}}(v) = 
d_{F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(v)\)
for every \(v\in A_1\), and \(d_{F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}}(v) = 
d_{F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(v)\)
for every \(v\in A_2\).

For every \(v\in A_i\) and every \(1\leq j\leq k-1\), 
we have \(d_{G'_i}(v)/(2k-1) = d_{F_{i,j}}(v)/2 = d^*(v)\).
Now, recall that for each \(v\in A_i\), we have \(d_{M_i}(v) = 
d^*(v)\). Therefore, for every \(v\in A_1\), we have 







$$\mathcal{B}'(v) = d_{G'_1}(v)/(2k-1) + d_{F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}}(v) 
			 = d^*(v) + d_{F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(v) 
			 = d_{M_1}(v)+ d_{F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(v) 
			 = |S_v|.$$


Similarly, we have $\mathcal{B}'(v)=|S_v|$ for every $v\in A_2$.
\end{proof}

As we have seen, we can extend every tracking \(B\) of 
\(\mathcal{B}'\) by adding one edge at
each end-vertex of \(B\). Let $\mathcal{B}$ be the tracking decomposition obtained by this 
extension. Since $\mathcal{B}'$ is a $(2k-1)$-path tracking decomposition and we added edges 
only at the end-vertices of these trackings, 
$\mathcal{B}$ is composed of trackings of vanilla \((2k+1)\)-trails. Furthermore, since we added all edges in 
\(E(G)-E(G')\), $\mathcal{B}$ is a decomposition of $G$.


\begin{claim}
\(\mathcal{B}\) is \(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
Fix \(x_0\in A_1\). First we will prove that  \(\mathcal{B}(x_0) \leq 
d_{F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(x_0) + d_{M_2}(x_0)\). If there is no tracking \(T = 
x_0x_1\cdots x_{2k+1}\) in \(\mathcal{B}\),
where \(x_0x_1\) is an edge of \(E(G) - E(G')\), then $\mathcal{B}(x_0)=0$. 
For every such tracking $T$, by the construction of $\mathcal{B}$, we know that \(x_0x_1\) is an 
element of \(S_{x_1}\).
Since \(x_1\) is a vertex of \(A_2\), we have \(S_{x_1} \subset M_2\cup 
F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}\).
Therefore,
\begin{equation*}
\mathcal{B}(x_0) \leq d_{F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(x_0) + d_{M_2}(x_0).
\end{equation*}

Now we will prove that \(\mathcal{B}(x_0) \geq d_{F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(x_0) + 
d_{M_2}(x_0)\). Note that, if \(x_0x_1\) is an edge of \(M_2\cup 
F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}\)
that is incident to \(x_0\) in \(A_1\) \big(these are the only edges of $G$ that 
can contribute to $\mathcal{B}(x_0)$\big), 
then, by the construction of $\mathcal{B}$, there is a tracking \(Q' = x_1\cdots x_{2k}\) in 
\(\mathcal{B}'\) of a path
such that the tracking \(Q = x_0x_1\cdots x_{2k+1}\) (of a vanilla trail) belongs to 
\(\mathcal{B}\).
Therefore \(\mathcal{B}(x_0) \geq d_{F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(x_0) + d_{M_2}(x_0)\), from where 
we conclude that
\(\mathcal{B}(v) = d_{F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(v) + d_{M_2}(v)\) for every \(v\) in \(A_1\).
Thus, for every vertex \(v\) in \(A_1\) we have 
\[
	\mathcal{B}(v)	= d_{F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(v) + d_{M_2}(v)
			= d^*(v) + d_{M_2}(v)
			= d_{G_1}(v)/(2k+1) + d_{M_2}(v).
\]
Analogously, we have \(\mathcal{B}(v) = d_{G_2}(v)/(2k+1) + d_{M_1}(v)\)
for each vertex \(v\) in \(A_2\).
Thus, \(\mathcal{B}\) is an \(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced $(2k+1)$-tracking decomposition.
\end{proof}

\begin{claim}
\(\mathcal{B}\) is \((2k+1)\)-pre-complete.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
Let \(v\in A_i\). We shall prove that \(\mathrm{preHang}(v,\mathcal{B}) > 2k+1\).
Note that, by the construction of $\mathcal{B}$, the set of pre-hanging edges at \(v\) in 
\(\mathcal{B}\) is exactly \(S_v\).
Then, \(\mathrm{preHang}(v,\mathcal{B}) = |S_v| = \mathcal{B}'(v)\).
Since \(\mathcal{B}'\) is balanced, \(\mathcal{B}'(v) \geq d_{G'_i}(v)/(2k-1)\).
Therefore,
\begin{equation*}
	\mathrm{preHang}(v,\mathcal{B})	= \mathcal{B}'(v) 
					\geq d_{G'_i}(v)/(2k-1) 
					= d^*(v) 
					= d_{G_i}(v)/(2k+1).
\end{equation*} 
Since \(\mathbb{F}\) is a strong \((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorization of \(G\),
we have \(d_{G_i}(v) \geq (2k+1)(2k+2)\), from where we conclude that 
\(\mathrm{preHang}(v,\mathcal{B}) \geq 2k+2\).
Therefore, \(\mathcal{B}\) is a \((2k+1)\)-pre-complete tracking decomposition.
\end{proof}
Now we are able to conclude the proof.
By Lemma~\ref{lemma:odd-complete}, \(G\) admits an 
\(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced
\((k+1)\)-complete $(2k+1)$-tracking decomposition.
By Lemma~\ref{lemma:odd-path-dec}, \(G\) admits an 
\(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced
\((k+1)\)-complete $(2k+1)$-path tracking decomposition.
Therefore, \(G\) admits an \(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced $(2k+1)$-path tracking decomposition.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $k$ from Lemma 5.2. Remove a matching and half of an oriented Eulerian factor to get a strong $(1,2k-1)$-bifactorization, decompose by induction, extend each path by one edge at each end, then apply Lemmas 5.3 and 5.4.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement:
The proof is by induction on \(k\).
By Lemma~\ref{lemma:3-PD}, the statement is true for \(k=1\).
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $k$; $k=1$ is Lemma 5.2.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Inductive setup
nodes.statement:
Thus, suppose \(k>1\),
and let \(G = (A_1,A_2;E)\) be a bipartite graph that admits a strong  
\((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorization \(\mathbb{F} = (\mathcal{F}_1,\mathcal{F}_2)\).
We claim that \(G\) admits an \(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced 
\((2k+1)\)-pre-complete 
$(2k+1)$-tracking decomposition.
Let \(\mathcal{F}_1 = \{M_1,F_{1,1},\ldots,F_{1,k}\}\) 
and \(\mathcal{F}_2 = \{M_2,F_{2,2},\ldots,F_{2,k}\}\),
and let \(G_i = G\big[\bigcup_{F\in\mathcal{F}_i} F\big]\) for \(i = 1,2\).
Hereafter, fix $i \in \{1,2\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a strong $(1,2k+1)$-bifactorization and aim for a balanced pre-complete tracking decomposition.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Orient a 2-factor
nodes.statement:
Define \(d^*(v) = 
d_{G_i}(v)/(2k+1)\) for every vertex \(v\) in \(A_i\).
Note that \(d_{F_{i,j}}(v) = 2d^*(v) = 2d_{M_i}(v)\) for every vertex \(v\) in 
\(A_i\) and \(1\leq j\leq k\). 
Let \(O_{F_{i,k}}\) be a Eulerian 
orientation of \(F_{i,k}\).
Let \(F_{i,k} = F_{i,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits} \cup F_{i,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}\), where 
\(F_{i,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}\) is the set of 
edges
of \(F_{i,k}\) leaving \(A_i\) in \(O_{F_{i,k}}\),
and \(F_{i,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}\) is the set of edges of \(F_{i,k}\) entering
\(A_i\)
in \(O_{F_{i,k}}\).
Note that, since \(O_{F_{i,k}}\) is an Eulerian orientation,
\(d_{F_{i,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(v) = d_{F_{i,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}}(v) = d_{F_{i,k}}(v)/2\) for 
every 
vertex \(v\in A_i\).
nodes.statement_short: Split $F_{i,k}$ via an Eulerian orientation into forward and backward halves.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Reduced graph G'
nodes.statement:
Let \(G' = G - M_1 - M_2 - F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits} - F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}\),
and define \(\mathcal{F}'_i = \{F_{i,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits},F_{i,1},\ldots, F_{i,k-1}\}\).
Let \(G'_i = G\big[\bigcup_{F\in\mathcal{F}'_i} F\big]\).
Note that \(G'_i = G_i - M_i - F_{i,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}\).
Then, for every vertex \(v\in A_i\), we have
\begin{equation} d_{G'_i}(v) = d_{G_i}(v) - 2d^*(v) 
	    = (2k+1)d^*(v) - 2d^*(v) 
	    = (2k-1)d^*(v).
\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Remove $M_i$ and forward halves; degrees on $A_i$ become $(2k-1)d^*(v)$.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Claim 5.6
nodes.statement:
\begin{claim}
\(\mathbb{F}' = (\mathcal{F}'_1,\mathcal{F}'_2)\) is a strong 
\((1,2k-1)\)-bifactorization of \(G'\).
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}

To prove this claim, we shall prove the following.
\begin{itemize}
	\item[(i)] \(F_{i,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}\) is an \((A_i,1,2k-1)\)-factor of 
\(G'_i\);
	\item[(ii)] \(F_{i,j}\) is an Eulerian \((A_i,2,2k-1)\)-factor 
			of \(G'_i\) for \(1\leq j\leq k-1\);
	\item[(iii)] \(d_{G'_i}(v) \geq (2k-1)(2k)\) for every vertex \(v\in 
A_i\).
\end{itemize}

To prove items (i) and (ii), first 
note that, for every $v\in A_i$, we have \(d_{F_{i,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}}(v) = 
d^*(v)\) and \(d_{F_{i,j}}(v) = 2d^*(v)\) for every \(1\leq 
j\leq k-1\). By~\eqref{odd-d}, we conclude that \(F_{i,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}\) is a 
\((A_i,1,2k-1)\)-factor of 
\(G'_i\) and \(F_{i,j}\) is an \((A_i,2,2k-1)\)-factor of \(G'_i\). 
Since \(\mathbb{F}\) is a \((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorization,
\(F_{1,j}\) and \(F_{2,j}\) are Eulerian graphs for 
\(1\leq j\leq k-1\).

It remains to prove item (iii).
Since \(d_{G'_i}(v) = (2k-1)d^*(v)\) and \(d^*(v) = d_{G_i}(v)/(2k+1)\) for 
every vertex \(v\in A_i\),
we have \(d_{G'_i}(v) = \frac{2k-1}{2k+1}d_{G_i}(v)\) for every \(v\in A_i\).
Since \(\mathbb{F}\) is a strong \((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorization, 
\(d_{G_i}(v) \geq (2k+1)(2k+2)\) for every \(v\in A_i\).
Therefore, \(d_{G'_i}(v) \geq (2k-1)(2k+2) > (2k-1)2k\) for every \(v\in 
A_i\).
\end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Claim 5.6 and its proof.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Apply induction
nodes.statement:
Since 
\(\mathbb{F}'\) is a strong \((1,2k-1)\)-bifactorization of \(G'\),
by the induction hypothesis, 
\(G'\) admits an \(\mathbb{F}'\)-balanced $(2k-1)$-path 
tracking decomposition \(\mathcal{B}'\).
nodes.statement_short: Induction gives a balanced $(2k-1)$-path decomposition $\mathcal{B}'$ of $G'$.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: End-counts of B'
nodes.statement:
Since \(\mathcal{B}'\) is a \(\mathbb{F}'\)-balanced $(2k-1)$-path tracking decomposition, we have
	\begin{itemize}
		\item \(\mathcal{B}'(v) = d_{G'_1}(v)/(2k-1) + d_{F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}}(v)\) 
for every 
\(v\in A_1\);
		\item \(\mathcal{B}'(v) = d_{G'_2}(v)/(2k-1) + d_{F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}}(v)\) 
for every 
\(v\in A_2\).
nodes.statement_short: Write out the end-counts of $\mathcal{B}'$.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Edge sets S_v
nodes.statement:
Now we want to extend each tracking in \(\mathcal{B}'\) to obtain 

a \((2k+1)\)-tracking decomposition of \(G\).
For that, we add edges from  
\(E(G) - E(G')\) at the end-vertices of the trackings in $\mathcal{B}'$.
For each \(v\in A_1\) (\(v\in A_2\)), let \(S_v\) be the set of edges of 
\(M_1\cup F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}\) (\(M_2\cup F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}\)) that are incident 
to \(v\).
Note that for each edge \(e\) in \(E(G) - E(G')\) 
there is exactly one \(v\in V(G)\) such that \(e\in S_v\).
Then, \(\bigcup_{v\in V(G)} S_v = E(G) - 
E(G')\).
Therefore, if we prove that \(\mathcal{B}'(v) = |S_v|\), then we can extend every 
tracking $B$ in $\mathcal{B}'$ by adding one edge at each end-vertex of $B$.
nodes.statement_short: Assign the removed edges to vertices as sets $S_v$; need $\mathcal{B}'(v)=|S_v|$.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Claim 5.7
nodes.statement:
\begin{claim}
	\(\mathcal{B}'(v) = |S_v|\), for every $v\in V(G)$.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
First, note that, since \(F_{i,k}\) is Eulerian, we have 
\(d_{F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}}(v) = 
d_{F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(v)\)
for every \(v\in A_1\), and \(d_{F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}}(v) = 
d_{F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(v)\)
for every \(v\in A_2\).

For every \(v\in A_i\) and every \(1\leq j\leq k-1\), 
we have \(d_{G'_i}(v)/(2k-1) = d_{F_{i,j}}(v)/2 = d^*(v)\).
Now, recall that for each \(v\in A_i\), we have \(d_{M_i}(v) = 
d^*(v)\). Therefore, for every \(v\in A_1\), we have 







$$\mathcal{B}'(v) = d_{G'_1}(v)/(2k-1) + d_{F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}}(v) 
			 = d^*(v) + d_{F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(v) 
			 = d_{M_1}(v)+ d_{F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(v) 
			 = |S_v|.$$


Similarly, we have $\mathcal{B}'(v)=|S_v|$ for every $v\in A_2$.
\end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Claim 5.7 and its proof.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Extend paths
nodes.statement:
As we have seen, we can extend every tracking \(B\) of 
\(\mathcal{B}'\) by adding one edge at
each end-vertex of \(B\). Let $\mathcal{B}$ be the tracking decomposition obtained by this 
extension. Since $\mathcal{B}'$ is a $(2k-1)$-path tracking decomposition and we added edges 
only at the end-vertices of these trackings, 
$\mathcal{B}$ is composed of trackings of vanilla \((2k+1)\)-trails. Furthermore, since we added all edges in 
\(E(G)-E(G')\), $\mathcal{B}$ is a decomposition of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Extend each path by one edge at each end to get a vanilla $(2k+1)$-trail decomposition $\mathcal{B}$.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Claim 5.8
nodes.statement:
\begin{claim}
\(\mathcal{B}\) is \(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
Fix \(x_0\in A_1\). First we will prove that  \(\mathcal{B}(x_0) \leq 
d_{F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(x_0) + d_{M_2}(x_0)\). If there is no tracking \(T = 
x_0x_1\cdots x_{2k+1}\) in \(\mathcal{B}\),
where \(x_0x_1\) is an edge of \(E(G) - E(G')\), then $\mathcal{B}(x_0)=0$. 
For every such tracking $T$, by the construction of $\mathcal{B}$, we know that \(x_0x_1\) is an 
element of \(S_{x_1}\).
Since \(x_1\) is a vertex of \(A_2\), we have \(S_{x_1} \subset M_2\cup 
F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}\).
Therefore,
\begin{equation*}
\mathcal{B}(x_0) \leq d_{F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(x_0) + d_{M_2}(x_0).
\end{equation*}

Now we will prove that \(\mathcal{B}(x_0) \geq d_{F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(x_0) + 
d_{M_2}(x_0)\). Note that, if \(x_0x_1\) is an edge of \(M_2\cup 
F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}\)
that is incident to \(x_0\) in \(A_1\) \big(these are the only edges of $G$ that 
can contribute to $\mathcal{B}(x_0)$\big), 
then, by the construction of $\mathcal{B}$, there is a tracking \(Q' = x_1\cdots x_{2k}\) in 
\(\mathcal{B}'\) of a path
such that the tracking \(Q = x_0x_1\cdots x_{2k+1}\) (of a vanilla trail) belongs to 
\(\mathcal{B}\).
Therefore \(\mathcal{B}(x_0) \geq d_{F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(x_0) + d_{M_2}(x_0)\), from where 
we conclude that
\(\mathcal{B}(v) = d_{F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(v) + d_{M_2}(v)\) for every \(v\) in \(A_1\).
Thus, for every vertex \(v\) in \(A_1\) we have 
\[
	\mathcal{B}(v)	= d_{F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(v) + d_{M_2}(v)
			= d^*(v) + d_{M_2}(v)
			= d_{G_1}(v)/(2k+1) + d_{M_2}(v).
\]
Analogously, we have \(\mathcal{B}(v) = d_{G_2}(v)/(2k+1) + d_{M_1}(v)\)
for each vertex \(v\) in \(A_2\).
Thus, \(\mathcal{B}\) is an \(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced $(2k+1)$-tracking decomposition.
\end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Claim 5.8 and its proof.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Claim 5.9
nodes.statement:
\begin{claim}
\(\mathcal{B}\) is \((2k+1)\)-pre-complete.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}
Let \(v\in A_i\). We shall prove that \(\mathrm{preHang}(v,\mathcal{B}) > 2k+1\).
Note that, by the construction of $\mathcal{B}$, the set of pre-hanging edges at \(v\) in 
\(\mathcal{B}\) is exactly \(S_v\).
Then, \(\mathrm{preHang}(v,\mathcal{B}) = |S_v| = \mathcal{B}'(v)\).
Since \(\mathcal{B}'\) is balanced, \(\mathcal{B}'(v) \geq d_{G'_i}(v)/(2k-1)\).
Therefore,
\begin{equation*}
	\mathrm{preHang}(v,\mathcal{B})	= \mathcal{B}'(v) 
					\geq d_{G'_i}(v)/(2k-1) 
					= d^*(v) 
					= d_{G_i}(v)/(2k+1).
\end{equation*} 
Since \(\mathbb{F}\) is a strong \((1,2k+1)\)-bifactorization of \(G\),
we have \(d_{G_i}(v) \geq (2k+1)(2k+2)\), from where we conclude that 
\(\mathrm{preHang}(v,\mathcal{B}) \geq 2k+2\).
Therefore, \(\mathcal{B}\) is a \((2k+1)\)-pre-complete tracking decomposition.
\end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Claim 5.9 and its proof.
nodes.section: 5 Decomposition into paths of odd length

nodes.name: Conclude via Lemmas 5.3, 5.4
nodes.statement:
Now we are able to conclude the proof.
By Lemma~\ref{lemma:odd-complete}, \(G\) admits an 
\(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced
\((k+1)\)-complete $(2k+1)$-tracking decomposition.
By Lemma~\ref{lemma:odd-path-dec}, \(G\) admits an 
\(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced
\((k+1)\)-complete $(2k+1)$-path tracking decomposition.
Therefore, \(G\) admits an \(\mathbb{F}\)-balanced $(2k+1)$-path tracking decomposition.
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas 5.3 and 5.4 turn $\mathcal{B}$ into a balanced path decomposition.

nodes.name: Three items

nodes.statement:

note that, for every $v\in A_i$, we have \(d_{F_{i,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}}(v) =

nodes.statement: \(\mathcal{B}'(v) = |S_v|\), for every $v\in V(G)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 5.7
nodes.statement:
First, note that, since \(F_{i,k}\) is Eulerian, we have 
\(d_{F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}}(v) = 
d_{F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(v)\)
for every \(v\in A_1\), and \(d_{F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}}(v) = 
d_{F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(v)\)
for every \(v\in A_2\).

$$\mathcal{B}'(v) = d_{G'_1}(v)/(2k-1) + d_{F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}}(v) 
			 = d^*(v) + d_{F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(v) 
			 = d_{M_1}(v)+ d_{F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(v) 
			 = |S_v|.$$

nodes.statement:
First, note that, since \(F_{i,k}\) is Eulerian, we have 
\(d_{F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}}(v) = 
d_{F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(v)\)
for every \(v\in A_1\), and \(d_{F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}}(v) =

for every \(v\in A_2\).

For every \(v\in A_i\) and every \(1\leq j\leq k-1\), 
we have \(d_{G'_i}(v)/(2k-1) = d_{F_{i,j}}(v)/2 = d^*(v)\).
Now, recall that for each \(v\in A_i\), we have \(d_{M_i}(v) = 
d^*(v)\).

Therefore, for every \(v\in A_1\), we have 







$$\mathcal{B}'(v) = d_{G'_1}(v)/(2k-1) + d_{F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm back}}\nolimits}}(v) 
			 = d^*(v) + d_{F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(v) 
			 = d_{M_1}(v)+ d_{F_{2,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}}(v)

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 5.8
nodes.statement:

F_{1,k}^{\mathop{\text{\rm forw}}\nolimits}\)
that is incident to \(x_0\) in \(A_1\) \big(these are the only edges of $G$ that

then, by the construction of $\mathcal{B}$, there is a tracking \(Q' = x_1\cdots x_{2k}\) in
